podcast.title: Critical Commentary (Ken Barnes, 1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Ken Barnes wrote that April Wine was overlooked by radio programmers, being considered "too hard for AM" but "not weighty enough for FM progressives." Reviewers scorned them for lacking a "convenient handle" like Bruce Springsteen's "street poetics," 10cc's "verbal manipulations," or The Rolling Stones' "historical legacy," causing record companies to neglect their promotion. "Reviewers scorn them because they don't have the convenient handle."

podcast.title: US Touring Decision (1977)
podcast.body: April Wine initially resisted touring the United States for a long time but eventually realized that touring was essential if they wanted to gain a larger American audience, leading to significant tours in 1977. "They had resisted touring the US for a long time, but they finally realized we have to if we want to get a larger American audience."

podcast.title: Gary Moffet on Canadian Inferiority Complex (1981)
podcast.body: In 1981, Gary Moffet of April Wine articulated the ongoing "inferiority complex" in Canada regarding its own bands, criticizing the perception that Canadian artists needed to succeed in the US before being respected at home. He questioned why Canadian judgment wasn't trusted independently of American approval. "Gary Moffet of the band April Wine was still talking about the perception that Canadian bands needed to make it in the US even in 1981. He said Canada has an inferiority complex because of it. They don't trust their own bands with enough respect. They don't perceive you as being really big unless you go away, improve yourself in America. Why should you have to do well away from home before your own people consider you a top band? That's silly. Canadians should trust their own judgment. They shouldn't need America's approval about something before they accept it."

podcast.title: Addition of a Third Guitarist
podcast.body: April Wine expanded its lineup by adding a third guitarist, a change that was noted for enhancing and "pumping up" their overall sound, contributing to their evolving musical direction. "And April Wine added a third guitarist which pumped up their sound."

podcast.title: Beneficiary of FM Radio Rules
podcast.body: April Wine was a band that benefited from Canada's changed FM radio rules in the 1960s, which required stations to play more album-oriented rock and a 30% Canadian content quota. This provided more airplay opportunities for established Canadian bands. "This helped out bands like Rush Triumph in April wine."

podcast.title: Canadian Success Before US Breakthrough
podcast.body: April Wine had already established a successful career in Canada before they managed to break through on American radio, highlighting their domestic popularity prior to international recognition efforts. "So by the time that April Wine broke through on American Radio, they already had a successful career in Canada."

podcast.title: Cancon Boosted Success (1970s)
podcast.body: April Wine was among the numerous Canadian rock bands whose careers were significantly helped by the Cancon rules in the 1970s, leading to both national success and, for some, international recognition. "Just on the rock side, we had Rush, April Wine, the Guess Who, Triumph, Crobar, Teenage Head, Max Webster, Chilowac, FM, Saga, and a foot-and-cold water."

podcast.title: Difficulty Being Labeled by American Radio
podcast.body: The band's particular brand of rock music made it challenging for them to be categorized, which led to American radio programmers being unsure how to effectively promote or feature their sound. "But their brand of rock made them hard to label and therefore American Radio was not sure what to do with them."

podcast.title: Early Success and Domestic Acceptance
podcast.body: April Wine had success as far back as the 1960s, but like many Canadian groups, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after they had a hit in America. This pattern highlights the historical bias where external validation was crucial for Canadian artists at home. "The guests who BTO Rush, Triumph, April Wine and others had success as far back as the 1960s. But in most cases, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after these groups had a hit in America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Early Hits
podcast.body: April Wine was formed in the late 1960s in Nova Scotia and achieved two hits in Canada in 1972: "Bad Side of the Moon" and "You Could Have Been a Lady." "April Wine formed back in the late 60s in Nova Scotia and they had a couple of hits in Canada in 1972, bad side of the moon. And you could have been a lady which is a cover of a great song by Hot Chocolate."

podcast.title: Impact of Myles Goodwyn's Death
podcast.body: The recent death of Myles Goodwyn was described as a terrible blow and a major influence on the speaker's early rock and roll life. The speaker was a big fan but had to listen to the band's music very quietly and by himself during his time at an alternative radio station in 1996, to avoid ostracization. "And the fact that Miles Goodwin died over the weekends, like, oh my God, that was a terrible blow because he was such a, you know, in major influence on my early rock and roll life."

podcast.title: Mid-1980s Domestic & International Success
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, April Wine was among several Canadian rock acts that released albums performing "extremely well domestically and internationally," some even achieving multi-platinum sales in foreign markets. "Rush, April Wine, BTO, Loverboy, Triumph, Brian Adams, and a half a dozen others all released albums that had done extremely well domestically and internationally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Pioneering Power Ballad Sound
podcast.body: As the 1970s transitioned into the 1980s, April Wine showcased a musical style that offered a preview of the power ballad, a genre that would become pervasive and inescapable throughout the 1980s. "As the 70s creep into the 80s, April Wine gives us a glimpse to what is in store for us, the power ballad."

podcast.title: Significant Influence
podcast.body: April Wine was a major influence on early rock and roll life for many. The recent passing of Myles Goodwyn was considered a "terrible blow" due to his profound impact on the rock music scene. "I was always a giant April wine fan."

podcast.title: Unnoticed by Record Buyers
podcast.body: As a direct consequence of record companies not knowing how to promote them and letting them "slide," April Wine went largely unnoticed by record buyers at large, despite their musical qualities. "And accordingly they go unnoticed by record buyers at large."
